newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - EU setback for Swedish alcohol monopoly.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EU setback for Swedish alcohol monopoly.

text.p: Sweden's state alcohol monopoly suffered a legal blow on Tuesday when an adviser at the European Court of Justice said European Union law was an "obstacle" to such retail sales regimes for alcohol.

The opinion of Advocate-General Michael Elmer represents a setback for Sweden, which has a monopoly on the retail sale of wines and spirits as well as other stringent liquor laws intended to keep down alcohol consumption.
Opinions by advocates-general are only advisory, but are often followed by the court in final rulings.
However, the Swedish government stressed that the issue had not yet been finally decided.
"It is too early to scrap the retail monopoly," Finance Minister Erik Asbrink told the Swedish news agency TT.

Ulf Bernitz, professor in European law at Stockholm University, said the alcohol retail monopoly -- Systembolaget -- could not keep its present position if the EU court also came to the conclusion that it constituted a trade barrier.
"Sweden's alcohol policies will sink if Sweden is forced to abolish the monopoly of Systembolaget," said Hans Lindqvist, a Swedish member of the European parliament.
However, Health & Social Affairs Minister Margot Wallstrom said that under "no circumstances" would the sale of alcohol beverages become totally free.
The case is also of interest for neigbouring Finland which has a similar alcohol retail monopoly.
It comes after the district court of the Swedish town of Landskrona asked the EU court for a preliminary ruling on whether the retail monopoly was compatible with EU law.
The Landskrona public prosecutor had brought legal action against grocer Harry Franzen for breaking the monopoly of Systembolaget over sales of wine and spirits.
Franzen started selling wine in his shop in 1994, determined to see if Sweden's strict alcohol rules broke EU law, but was soon was soon ordered to stop by the police.
"Of course, this is a victory," Franzen told the Swedish news agency TT about the opinion of the EU advocate-general.
The Landskrona court has asked the EU court to rule on whether the Swedish alcohol monopoly was compatible with EU legislation which, for example, bans quantitative restrictions on imports.

In his opinion, Elmer said EU rules were an obstacle to national systems which aim to restrict sales by giving a state company the sole right to alcohol retail sales and in which the monopoly is the only lawful buyer for the retail market, in practice also deciding which products should be imported.

Such a system could not be justified on the grounds of protecting people's health as this could be taken into consideration through measures which did not restrict the free movement of goods to the same extent, Elmer said.
No date has yet been set for the ruling by the EU court.
